synopsis: ISO/TS 21815-2:2021 was published in July 2021 and confirmed in December 2024; it defines the on-board SAE J1939 interface through which a collision-avoidance device requests slowing, stopping or prevention of machine motion [f10725, f2057, f2158]. Its commands distinguish controlled stops from emergency stops, include motion inhibit and prevention of movement from standstill, and exclude automatic steering; the interface also includes capability discovery and a keep-alive signal [f3638, f6237, f3639, f12979]. The interface is explicitly not plug-and-play: manufacturers must agree integration details, machines may report that actions can be overridden, and validation must include end-to-end integration latency [f2159, f6238, f8198]. Vendor precedents include Epiroc's 2021 implementation using a draft interface and Bell's August 2023 statement that Pin 3 E-series ADTs support third-party PDS or CAS integration up to Level 9 through a gateway [f1348, f1839, f1391]. Across chapters, the interface anchors brake requests, evidence reuse and HIL testing; a production-relevant HIL bench could target mid-2027, but should stay off the critical path unless ECU, bus and actuator interfaces stabilise early [f5579, f367, f538, f857]. Planning should include interoperability demonstrations and interface tests, while acknowledging that the review found no simulation provisions, did not review interface-conformance testing content, and reports the specification's warning that collision-avoidance algorithms are not yet mature and well understood [f10726, f11078, f9780, f2661, f8934].

relations.note: Both identify the standardized interface as a precedent for cross-model evidence reuse.
Both report Bell E-series readiness for third-party systems up to Level 9.
Together specify July 2021 publication and December 2024 confirmation.
Both describe slow, stop and motion-prevention commands; the latter specifies standstill.
Both require additional integration details and explicitly reject plug-and-play implementation.
The glossary repeats the specification's non-plug-and-play limitation.
Both quote the introduction's warning about immature, poorly understood algorithms.
Both anchor the booklet's brake request in the J1939 interface.
Both identify HIL as the natural test setting for this intervention interface.
The glossary adds capability discovery and keep-alive signaling to the command description.
Emergency-stop semantics explain one side of the emergency-versus-controlled-stop distinction.
Interface emulation capability supports choosing HIL as the natural test setting.
A production-relevant HIL target depends on the required simulator, models and interfaces.
Machine-specific integration requirements justify validating end-to-end interface latency.
Existing site-system compatibility risks motivate demonstrations of interoperability.
MOSH's laboratory interface bench test supports HIL's role in South African verification.
The Epiroc case adds tagging of all people and machines to the draft-interface implementation.
Unreviewed conformance testing limits interpretation of the review's missing simulation provisions.
